Issued at 106 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

This afternoon - Tonight: Low Thunderstorm Potential

A weak 500hPa shortwave trough has been moving northeastward 
throughout the morning and has made its way into the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley this afternoon. An unstable atmosphere 
exists across the region given the warm conditions today with 
MUCAPE values of 2000-3000 J/kg analyzed. Effective bulk shear 
of 35-40 kts is also depicted, strongest north of I-90 where 
500hPa wind speeds associated with a closed low moving eastward 
across the United States/Canada border are maximized. However, 
fairly strong capping exists across much of the area, especially
south of I-90 where boundary layer dry air depicted in model 
soundings has largely kept convection at bay through the morning
hours. 

This capping decreases with northward extent given increasing 
low level moisture ahead of an approaching surface front. 
Forcing along the front combined with the northeastward moving 
wave should be able to develop some showers and storms across 
the region late this afternoon into this evening (10-30%) given 
the favorable instability and shear profiles. Areas east of the
Mississippi River and north of I-90 have the greatest potential
to see a shower or storm though thinking the bulk of any 
convective activity, and with it the potential of a stronger 
storm, will exist northeast of our area where low level capping 
is minimized. 

Given the high humidity across the region, some valley fog 
development seems reasonable overnight, possibly spilling out 
into surrounding areas. The 31.12z HREF suggests 30-50% 
probabilities for visibilities less than 3SM across the region 
although partly cloudy skies could hinder more widespread 
development. Regardless, the typically foggy river valleys 
should see some visibility restrictions heading into Tuesday 
morning.

Tuesday: Shower/Storms South of I-90, Dry to the North

A bit of a bimodal weather scenario is expected Tuesday 
afternoon. The previously mentioned surface front stalls out 
generally just south of Minnesota/Iowa border where pooling 
surface moisture along the boundary will allow dewpoints to 
remain in the upper 60s to low 70s, building MUCAPE values 
upwards of 3000 J/kg once again. 500hPa winds remain maximized 
over the Upper Midwest throughout the day, resulting in 
effective bulk shear values of 35-40kts remaining across the
region and leading to another environment favorable for 
convective development. However, there remains the issue of low 
level capping and whether or not parcels can ascend through said 
cap. There appears to be an overall lack of a sufficient forcing
mechanism, but with the front in the vicinity, some isolated 
storms appear possible across our far southern counties 
(10-30%). Some of these storms could become strong to 
potentially severe with gusty winds and hail being the main 
concerns. 

North of the boundary, drier conditions are expected as lower 
dewpoints are ushered into the region. Tuesday could be a fairly
efficient mixing day for these areas as RAP/HRRR soundings 
depict a pretty stout dry layer up to 500hPa. Cloud cover will 
be the main limiting factor to deeper mixing through Tuesday 
afternoon with these same soundings suggesting mixing tops out 
around 800hPa. However, if skies are clearer or turbulent 
mixing atop the boundary layer is more efficient than currently 
expected, deeper mixing is possible resulting in minimum RHs 
bottoming out in the 15-20 percent range per the 31.12z HREF. 

Wednesday - Friday: Daily Storm Chances and Warm

Several additional chances for storms exists across the region 
through the remainder of the week as several shortwave impulses
traverse the top of a ridge axis situated from the Southeast 
United States into the Upper Midwest. Wednesday morning is the 
next most favorable time for a wetting rain across the region 
(40-70%) although recent runs of the GEFS/EPS/GEPS has begun to 
suggest the higher probabilities exist across central Minnesota 
into northwest Wisconsin. If this trend continues, the bulk of 
any precipitation may miss our area. However, there is signal 
within these ensembles for rainfall amounts upwards of 1/2 
inch nudging into southeast Minnesota and western Wisconsin 
(10-30%), mainly north of I-90.

Early thursday morning brings another round of rainfall, this 
time further south. Probabilities for rainfall in the 31.13z NBM
are 40-70% across the entire region though highest along I-90. 
Friday morning looks to be fairly rinse and repeat of Wednesday 
and Thursday with current probabilities for rain sitting around 
40-60%. 

Can't rule out some rumbles of thunder with the rainfall any of
these mornings as at least a few hundred J/kg of MUCAPE look to
be present. Some of the AI/ML severe guidance even suggest the 
parameter space could support some stronger storms, though these
details are murky at best.
